# Studio standard — garaku-yard

The **Always** section is injected into every agent session at start, ahead of
the repository's own rules. Everything after it is reference for specific work.

## Always

- **Conventional Commits:** `type(scope): subject`. Types `feat` `fix` `docs`
  `test` `refactor` `chore` `build` `perf` `ci`; scope optional; `!` before the
  colon for a breaking change. Subject imperative, lowercase, no trailing
  period, about 72 characters at most. Check the message with
  `orbit commit-check <message-file>` before committing.
- **Branch + PR for all work**, unless the repository's conventions label a
  deviation. Name the branch `<type>/<slug>` with a commit type. An agent
  pushes the branch and opens or updates the PR; a person reviews and merges.
  Never push to `main`, merge, or force-push a branch under review.
- **One logical change per commit.** Run the repository's tests and formatters
  for what you touched first.
- **No `Co-Authored-By` trailer.** Never override git identity (no
  `git -c user.*`, no `--author`).
- **At a genuine fork, ask.** If the choices lead to materially different work
  and no convention settles it, do the independent work first, then use
  `ask_teammate` (or `orbit ask`). Otherwise decide and say what you decided.

## Git

- **Conventional Commits**: `type(scope): subject`.
  - **type** — `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `test`, `refactor`, `chore`, `build`,
    `perf`, `ci`. `!` for breaking (`refactor(sim)!: …`).
  - **scope** — optional; skip when the change is repo-wide.
  - **subject** — imperative, lowercase, no trailing period, ≤ ~72 chars.
- **Work on a branch, open a PR.** Feature/topic branch → PR → merge to `main`.
  Don't push straight to `main`.
- **Branch names carry a commit type**: `<type>/<slug>` (`feat/potato-arc`,
  `fix/collapse-cause-contract`, `docs/pr-workflow`), chosen when cutting the
  branch, not at PR time. A name copied from recent branches drifts as soon as
  one breaks the pattern, which is why it is written down.
- **The agent opens the PR; a person reviews and merges.** An agent commits,
  pushes its branch, and opens or updates the pull request. It never pushes to
  `main`, never merges, and never force-pushes a branch under review. The
  review gate is the point, and merge is where it sits.
- **One logical change per commit.** Run tests + format before committing.
- **No `Co-Authored-By` trailer** for AI-assisted commits.
- **Never override git identity** (no `git -c user.*`) — read the machine's
  ambient config. Two people + Claude share one identity surface.

The shared `orbit commit-check` command validates the machine-checkable parts
of this commit format in a local `commit-msg` hook and CI. It checks type,
optional scope and breaking marker, an initially lowercase subject, whitespace,
and a missing trailing period. The approximately 72-character target,
imperative wording, logical scope, and whether a co-author is an AI still need
human or agent judgment. `orbit agent setup --hooks` installs the hook if the
slot is free; it never replaces another hook.

> A repo may state a deliberate, temporary deviation from the git standard in its
> own section below — with the reason. Deviations are the exception and are
> expected to expire; the standard above is the norm.

## Versions and releases

> **Who this binds.** A repo with **consumers** versions; one without does not
> have to. The studio has exactly one producer today — `attractor-core`, pinned
> by `attractor-zero` at `0.19.0` — and a tag there is how a consumer states
> which behaviour it was built against, and how `Orbit.Deps.drift/1` can see a
> consumer fall behind. A repo nobody depends on tags when it is useful and
> skips it when it is not. Recorded 2026-09-02, because this section had read as
> a blanket rule while the repo it actually binds carried no copy of it.

- **Semver tags, `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`.** Annotated (`git tag -a`), so the tag
  carries a date and an author. `-rc.N` for prereleases (`v0.13.0-rc.3`).
- **The leading digit is a stability commitment, not a milestone count.** `1.0.0`
  says "there is a contract here; breaking it bumps major". A repo that commits
  freely to `main` and reshapes its own API stays in **0.x** — which is where all
  three repos currently are, honestly.
- **Milestone talk is not version talk.** "v2 of the board" is a *phase* of work
  and must not be read as `2.0.0`. When a repo's prose says "v1 complete", that
  is a milestone. Say "milestone" in prose if there is any chance of confusion —
  this collision is why Orbit went to `v0.2.0` and not `v2.0.0`.
- **One version per repo**, even in a monorepo. Tag the repo, not the component:
  no `cli/v0.2.0` / `server/v0.3.0` split while the parts ship together from one
  commit. Per-component tags assert an independence that a single release script
  exists to prevent, and they buy a compatibility matrix nobody wants to own.
  Revisit only when parts genuinely ship on separate schedules, or gain
  consumers who upgrade on their own.
- **A second product in the same repo gets a tag prefix**, released on its own
  schedule (`templates/vX.Y.Z` beside Orbit's plain `vX.Y.Z`). Anything that
  asks git for the repo's main version then uses `git describe --match 'v[0-9]*'`.
- **A release is titled with its version and nothing else.** `v0.2.0` — not
  `v0.2.0 — some evocative phrase`. The releases list is read as a version
  ladder, and a column of bare versions scans instantly; a subtitle makes it
  ragged and duplicates the first line of the notes, which is right there when
  you open it. The narrative goes in the body. (`gh release create v0.x.y` takes
  the title from the tag name if you omit `--title` entirely.)
- **A tag names a commit; the build stamps the commit.** Where a repo publishes
  binaries, the *commit* is what decides "am I current" — it is written by the
  build itself and cannot drift from the artifact. The *tag* is the human name,
  used in release notes and conversation. Never make a tag the currency check:
  tagging is a manual act and can lag, move, or be forgotten.

| repo | scheme | notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| attractor-core | `v0.x.y`, `-rc.N` | the longest tag history |
| attractor-zero | `v0.x.y` | changelog is date-keyed, not version-keyed |
| orbit | `v0.x.y` | tag + build-stamped commit; see below |

## Docs

- **Docs live in `.orbit/docs/`.** Every repo carries the folder; Orbit's wiki,
  `orbit sync`, and the brief all read from it. (The wiki falls back to a plain
  top-level `docs/` for a repo that hasn't adopted `.orbit/`, but `.orbit/docs/`
  is the convention.)
- **The spine** — the ordered doc set every repo is expected to carry:
  `overview` · `architecture` · `brand` · `conventions` · `glossary` ·
  `roadmap` · `runbook`, plus a **`decisions/`** folder for ADRs. `changelog` is
  recognized when present. The wiki renders unwritten spine docs as *slots to
  fill*, not errors — a small repo can leave some blank without it reading as a
  fault.
- **Where a document goes** (ADR 0026): a decision people should follow →
  `decisions/` (in force until superseded); what was found or done at a point
  in time → `log/YYYY-MM-DD-<slug>.md` (true as of its date, never edited
  afterwards); anything else describes how things are now → the spine, or
  `reference/` for longer current specifications.
- **History may grow; what agents load must stay small.** `log/` and
  `decisions/` are never pruned. `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` hold orientation, not
  status, and a `## Always` section holds only rules for every change.
- **No `progress` doc.** "Where this repo stands" is the per-repo **memo**
  (written at the end of a working session, surfaced on the brief), not a doc you
  hand-maintain. The memo replaced the old phase/health narrative.
- **Public files stay at the repository root.** `README.md`, `LICENSE`,
  `CONTRIBUTING`, `SECURITY` and `.github/` live where GitHub and contributors
  expect them. `.orbit/docs/` is the internal layer: it points to them and
  never moves or copies them.
- **Standalone `.html` briefs** (data-dense findings, decision briefs) may live
  anywhere under `.orbit/docs/`; the wiki renders them in a sandbox. Prose docs
  are markdown.

## Engineering judgment

The calls that keep a codebase from bloating:

- **Rule of three before extracting.** A pattern needs three concrete
  appearances before it becomes a shared module; two copies stay duplicated.
  Don't generalise across features that only look similar: concrete beats
  abstract. When something does deserve reuse, keep the shared part minimal
  and let each caller own its configuration.
- **Fix root causes, not symptoms.** No feedback that does nothing and no fake
  success. If tests fail, say so.
- **Defer explicitly.** A large item left for later becomes an Orbit task,
  never a silent skip.

## Asking a teammate

- **At a genuine fork, ask — don't guess, and don't stall.** When a product, UX
  or architecture call can't be settled from the repo, the code, or a stated
  preference, offer `ask_teammate` (Claude) or `orbit ask` (a person) and wait
  for the answer. ADR 0014.
- **"Genuine" is the calibration, and it is deliberately narrow.** Two tests,
  both required: the available answers lead to *materially different work*, and
  *no conventional default settles it*. A choice with an obvious default is not
  a fork — make it, say you made it, and carry on. An affordance that
  interrupts on every judgment call is one people learn to dismiss, which costs
  more than never having it.
- **Ask at the right moment, not the first moment.** Do everything that doesn't
  depend on the answer first, then ask once, naming the options and what each
  costs. A question that arrives with the rest of the work already done is
  cheap to answer; one that arrives instead of any work is an interruption.
- **Asking is cheap even when the answer isn't immediate.** An unanswered
  question parks rather than failing, and resurfaces next session through the
  read arrow — so the cost of asking when nobody is about is a delay, not a
  loss.

## Verified claims

A number copied out of a machine into prose can only ever drift one way: the
machine moves and the sentence doesn't. `roadmap.md` claimed a win on day 257
when the binary said 258 — a recalibration had moved it and nobody edited the
doc — and `CLAUDE.md` claimed a dependency at 0.11.0 against a project pinning
0.13.0. Both were settled in a second by running the command that produced them.

So a line can cite what backs it:

```markdown
The sim reaches the Proof on **day 258** <!-- orbit:verify ./run --winnable -->
```

`orbit verify` re-runs each command and checks the line still contains what it
prints — no duplicated expected value, the output *is* the expectation. It exits
non-zero on disagreement, so CI can gate on it, and `orbit verify --list` shows
what would run without running anything.

**Annotate sparingly.** Only numbers that (a) came from a command and (b) would
mislead someone if wrong. Annotating everything turns prose into configuration
and nobody maintains it.

Nothing runs these automatically — not the poller, not a hook. They execute only
when a person types `orbit verify`, in their own checkout, where the trust is
the same as a Makefile's.
